rows.verified: Workplaces need plans for emergencies such as serious injury, explosion, flood, poisoning, electrocution, fire, radioactive release and chemical spills.
Quick and effective action can reduce the consequences of workplace emergencies.
People respond more reliably when trained, competent and involved in regular realistic practice using agreed and rehearsed plans.
A written emergency plan is needed where a major incident could involve risks to the public, employee rescue or coordination of emergency services.
Employers sharing a workplace should consider coordinating emergency plans and procedures.
Emergency exits and escape routes must be sufficient, unobstructed and clearly marked, with suitable emergency lighting.
Competent people and other key incident-control roles should be nominated in advance.
Plans should cover shutdown or isolation actions and training for everyone, including people with disabilities and vulnerable workers.
Emergency controls depend on site hazards, occupancy, shift patterns, layout, alarm coverage, escape routes, responder access, communications and exercises.
Emergency-procedure evidence is incident-, site-, occupancy- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level consequence probability.
Employers must make sure employees receive immediate help if they are injured or become ill at work.
Workplace first-aid duties apply to every workplace and to self-employed people.
A suitably stocked first-aid kit must be provided.
An appointed person or people must take charge of first-aid arrangements.
Employees must be given information about workplace first-aid arrangements.
A first-aid needs assessment determines the equipment, facilities and personnel that should be provided.
The need for trained first-aiders and their training level depends on the nature and location of the work.
First-aid certificates used for workplace competence last three years and annual refresher training is strongly recommended.
First-aid provision depends on workplace hazards, workforce size and distribution, operating hours, vulnerable people, remoteness and emergency-service access.
First-aid evidence is workplace-, workforce-, hazard- and response-specific and is not an exact parcel-level survival or injury probability.
